# Acute heart failure

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Heart failure > Acute heart failure*

[Original Article Link](/library/Aq0Rah)

---

## Summary

Acute <u>heart failure</u> is the rapid onset or worsening of <u>heart failure symptoms</u>, and it is a common cause of hospitalization in older patients. Multiple triggers can cause an acute decompensation of preexisting <u>heart failure</u> (<u>ADHF</u>) but the condition may also occur suddenly in patients with no previous history of the condition (<u>de novo heart failure</u>). Diagnosis is based on typical clinical features (e.g., <u>dyspnea</u>), laboratory findings (e.g., elevated <u>BNP</u>), and imaging findings (e.g., <u>pulmonary edema</u>). Management is often challenging because of comorbidities; most patients require admission for treatment with IV <u>diuretics</u>, <u>vasodilators</u>, adjustment of their chronic <u>heart failure</u> (HF) medications, <u>respiratory support</u>, and careful monitoring.

---

## Definitions

* Acute decompensated heart failure (<u>ADHF</u>): An acute worsening of symptoms in a patient with preexisting <u>heart failure</u> (most common) [[2]](/library/lxYv9r)

* De novo heart failure: AHF symptoms occurring for the first time in a patient without known <u>heart failure</u> (∼ 15% of cases) [[2]](/library/lxYv9r)[[3]](/library/5xYiCr)[[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)

---

## Etiology

| Etiology of acute heart failure |  |
| --- | --- |
| Type of acute <u>heart failure</u> | <br>Underlying etiology [[2]](/library/lxYv9r)[[5]](/library/-RbDpt)<br> |
| <u>De novo heart failure</u> | <br><br>* Acute <u>myocardial</u> dysfunction<br><br>* Cardiac <u>ischemia</u> due to <u>acute coronary syndrome</u> (<u>ACS</u>)<br><br>* <u>Myocarditis</u><br><br>* Drug-induced <u>cardiomyopathy</u>  [[6]](/library/mxYVCr)<br><br>* <u>Peripartum cardiomyopathy</u><br><br>* <u>Thyroid storm</u><br><br>* <u>Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy</u><br><br>* <u>Takotsubo cardiomyopathy</u><br><br>* Acquired valvular pathology<br><br>* Acute <u>mitral regurgitation</u> after <u>ACS</u><br><br>* Bacterial <u>endocarditis</u><br><br>* <u>Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis</u><br><br>* Extracardiac pathologies that affect <u>left ventricular</u> output<br><br>* <u>Pulmonary embolus</u><br><br>* <u>Pericardial effusion</u> causing tamponade<br><br>* <u>Aortic dissection</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>ADHF</u> | <br><br>* Uncontrolled and/or refractory <u>hypertension</u> (see “<u>Hypertensive emergencies</u>”)<br><br>* New/worsening cardiac <u>ischemia</u><br><br>* <u>Arrhythmias</u> (e.g., <u>atrial fibrillation with RVR</u>, <u>complete heart block</u>)<br><br>* Serious infection/<u>sepsis</u> (e.g., <u>pneumonia</u>)<br><br>* Drugs<br><br>* Nonadherence to <u>heart failure</u> medication<br><br>* <u>NSAID</u> use<br><br>* Drugs with negative <u>inotropic</u> properties (e.g., <u>nondihydropyridine CCBs</u>) [[3]](/library/5xYiCr)<br><br>* Starting or uptitrating <u>beta blockers</u>  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)<br><br>* <u>Thiazolidinediones</u><br><br>* <u>Recreational substance</u> use, e.g., <u>cocaine</u>, <u>alcohol</u>, <u>methamphetamines</u><br><br>* <u>Anemia</u><br><br>* <u>Renal failure</u><br><br>* <u>Volume overload</u>, e.g., due to inappropriate fluid/salt intake or <u>IV fluid therapy</u><br><br>* In 40–50% of cases, no trigger is found.<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Consider <u>COVID-19</u> infection as a potential cause in both <u>de novo heart failure</u> and <u>ADHF</u>. [[8]](/library/2vcTzV0)

---

## Clinical features

<u>Clinical features of acute heart failure</u> are commonly classified according to <u>perfusion</u> and the presence of congestion at rest. [[2]](/library/lxYv9r)[[3]](/library/5xYiCr)[[7]](/library/-p1DH30)




| <br>Classification of acute heart failure [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br>No evidence of congestion (∼5% of patients) <br> | <br>Evidence of congestion (∼95% of patients) <br> |
| <br>Adequate <u>perfusion</u><br> | <br>* Warm and dry<br><br> | <br>* Warm and wet<br><br> |
| <br><u>Hypoperfusion</u><br> | <br>* Cold and dry<br><br> | <br>* Cold and wet<br><br> |





* Congestion (most common)  [[2]](/library/lxYv9r)[[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)

* <u>Clinical features of left heart failure</u>

* Acute <u>dyspnea</u> and <u>orthopnea</u> (i.e., worse when <u>supine</u>)

* <u>Signs of increased work of breathing</u> (<u>WOB</u>)

* <u>Cough</u> (occasionally with frothy, blood-tinged <u>sputum</u>)

* Coarse <u>crackles</u>/<u>rales</u> (and occasionally <u>wheezing</u>) on <u>lung auscultation</u>

* <u>S3 gallop</u> on <u>heart auscultation</u>

* Severe cases: central <u>cyanosis</u>

* <u>Clinical features of right heart failure</u>

* <u>Jugular venous distention</u>

* <u>Hepatojugular reflux</u>

* <u>Peripheral edema</u>

* <u>Ascites</u>

* <u>Flash pulmonary edema</u>: Typically manifests with <u>hypertension</u>, <u>pulmonary congestion</u>, and minimal <u>peripheral edema</u>

* <u>Hypoperfusion</u>

* <u>Weakness</u>, fatigue, <u>altered mental status</u>

* <u>Signs of poor peripheral perfusion</u>;  (e.g., cold, clammy <u>skin</u>, <u>peripheral cyanosis</u>, <u>skin</u> mottling)

* See also “<u>Cardiogenic shock</u>.”

* Blood pressure: may be low, normal, or elevated and should be interpreted in relation to the patient's baseline blood pressure





> [!TIP]
> The combined presence of <u>jugular venous distention</u>, <u>S3 gallop</u>, and <u>lung</u> <u>crackles</u>/<u>rales</u> makes a <u>diagnosis of acute heart failure</u> highly likely. [[10]](/library/LEcwwV0)




> [!TIP]
> Assess for clinical features that are suggestive of <u>hypoperfusion</u> (e.g., narrow <u>pulse pressure</u>, cool extremities, <u>peripheral cyanosis</u>, <u>altered mental status</u>, below baseline blood pressure) to identify patients with or at risk of <u>cardiogenic shock</u>. [[3]](/library/5xYiCr)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach




<u>Diagnosis of AHF</u> is primarily clinical.




* Obtain a <u>BNP</u> or <u>NT-proBNP</u> level in all patients.

* Obtain <u>CXR</u> and/or <u>lung POCUS</u> to confirm and evaluate <u>pulmonary congestion</u>.

* Order <u>ECG</u> and <u>laboratory studies</u> (e.g., <u>troponin</u>, <u>BMP</u>, <u>CBC</u>) to investigate underlying conditions (e.g., <u>ACS</u>) and/or differential diagnoses.

* Consider <u>POCUS for acute heart failure</u> to confirm diagnosis and guide management. [[11]](/library/stdtU70)

* Consult cardiology for early <u>TTE</u> for <u>ADHF</u> with a suspected decline in cardiac function OR any <u>de novo heart failure</u>.

* Investigate possible triggers (e.g., missed medications, <u>drugs that may worsen HF</u>, <u>clinical features of ACS</u>, infections).





### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




#### <u>BNP</u> or <u>NT-proBNP</u> [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[12]](/library/ra1fN20)[[13]](/library/aKWQUm0)




* Useful for diagnostic confirmation and prognosis

* Should be interpreted in the context of the patient's baseline level, history, <u>physical examination</u>, and imaging studies

* Can be measured serially to guide therapy





| <br><u>BNP</u> and <u>NT-proBNP</u> in acute <u>heart failure</u> [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[13]](/library/aKWQUm0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Heart failure</u> unlikely | <u>Heart failure</u> likely |
| <u>BNP</u> (pg/mL) | <br>* < 100<br><br> | <br>* > 400<br><br> |
| <u>NT-proBNP</u> (pg/mL) | <br>* < 300<br><br> | <br><br>* Age < 50 years: > 450<br><br>* Age 50–75 years: > 900<br><br>* Age > 75 years: > 1,800<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>BNP</u> has a high diagnostic value when combined with <u>physical examination</u> and imaging findings and is especially helpful in patients with an unclear diagnosis.




> [!WARNING]
> In a patient presenting with acute <u>dyspnea</u>, low <u>BNP</u> or <u>NT-proBNP</u> makes a <u>diagnosis of acute heart failure</u> very unlikely.




#### Additional blood tests




* <u>Troponin</u>: to rule out <u>ACS</u> [[14]](/library/n_c7KU0)

* <u>BMP</u>: to assess for <u>AKI</u> and/or <u>electrolyte</u> disturbances [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

* <u>CBC</u>: to assess for <u>anemia</u> [[15]](/library/vCYAFr)

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>: to assess for <u>congestive hepatopathy</u> or <u>ischemic</u> <u>hepatitis</u> [[16]](/library/lAcvPU0)

* Serum <u>albumin</u>: to assess for other <u>causes of peripheral edema</u>  [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)

* Consider <u>thyroid function tests</u>.  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[17]](/library/GzbB8w)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Troponin</u> levels are usually mildly elevated and stable in acute <u>heart failure</u>. In <u>ACS</u>, <u>troponin</u> levels rise rapidly and subsequently decline.




### <u>ECG</u>




* Indication: all patients to assess for <u>ACS</u>, <u>arrhythmias</u>, and conduction abnormalities

* ECG findings in acute heart failure are variable and may include: [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)

* Acute <u>ischemic</u> changes due to <u>ACS</u> (see “<u>Diagnosis of myocardial infarction</u>.”)

* <u>Atrial fibrillation</u>

* <u>Left ventricular hypertrophy</u>

* <u>Bundle branch block</u>

* Nonspecific <u>ST segment</u> changes

* Low <u>voltage</u> QRS  [[18]](/library/DCY18r)[[19]](/library/wCYh8r)

* <u>ECG</u> findings may be normal.





### Initial imaging




All patients with suspected acute <u>heart failure</u> should have a <u>chest x-ray</u> and <u>echocardiography</u> performed.  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[11]](/library/stdtU70)




#### <u>Chest x-ray</u> [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[20]](/library/yCYdur)



* Chest x-ray findings in cardiogenic pulmonary edema

* Enlarged <u>heart</u> shadow due to <u>cardiomegaly</u> and/or <u>pericardial effusion</u> [[21]](/library/EA08li)

* <u>Kerley B lines</u> (also known as <u>septal lines</u>)

* Prominent pulmonary vessels and perihilar alveolar edema (the hilar shadow has a butterfly or “bat wing” appearance)

* Basilar <u>interstitial</u> <u>edema</u>

* Bilateral <u>pleural effusions</u>  [[22]](/library/ESb8Yt)

* Cephalization: increased prominence of pulmonary vessels in the upper lobes of the <u>lungs</u> due to venous congestion [[23]](/library/rSbfat)

* <u>Peribronchial cuffing</u>




> [!NOTE]
> ABCDE: Alveolar <u>edema</u> (<u>bat wings</u>), Kerley B lines (<u>interstitial</u> <u>edema</u>), Cardiomegaly, Dilated prominent pulmonary vessels, and Effusions

#### <u>Transthoracic echocardiogram</u> (<u>TTE</u>) [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[24]](/library/KSbU0t)




* Indications: all patients with suspected acute <u>heart failure</u> (imaging modality of choice) [[25]](/library/LSbwZt)

* Characteristic echocardiographic findings of AHF

* Reduced or normal <u>LVEF</u> [[26]](/library/oSb00t)

* <u>Diastolic dysfunction</u>

* Left atrial dilation, valvular disorders  [[24]](/library/KSbU0t)

* <u>Pericardial effusion</u>

* <u>Right ventricular</u> <u>systolic dysfunction</u>, increase in <u>right ventricular</u> systolic pressure

* Specific findings related to underlying etiology

* Acute <u>myocardial</u> <u>ischemia</u>: regional wall motion abnormalities, <u>papillary muscle rupture</u>, <u>mitral valve regurgitation</u>, septal or <u>ventricular free wall rupture</u> [[25]](/library/LSbwZt)

* <u>Endocarditis</u>: vegetation on the valve

* See “Diagnostics” in “<u>Pulmonary embolism</u>.”

* See “Diagnostics” in “<u>Takotsubo cardiomyopathy</u>.”

#### POCUS in acute heart failure




* Description: bedside <u>ultrasound</u> of the <u>lung</u> fields, <u>inferior vena cava</u> (<u>IVC</u>), and <u>heart</u> 

* Can be used to assess <u>volume status</u> prior to and during treatment

* Higher diagnostic <u>accuracy</u> than chest <u>x-ray</u> combined with <u>NT-proBNP</u> [[11]](/library/stdtU70)[[27]](/library/cibaqt)

* Technique: See “<u>Focused cardiac ultrasound</u>.”

* Characteristic findings [[28]](/library/ACYRur)[[29]](/library/_CY5ur)[[30]](/library/aibQJt)[[31]](/library/bibHJt)

* <u>Lung</u> fields

* <u>Pleural effusions</u>

* ≥ 3 <u>B lines</u> in ≥ 2 bilateral <u>lung</u> zones suggest <u>pulmonary edema</u>   [[32]](/library/NAc-PU0)

* <u>IVC ultrasound</u>: diameter ≥ 2–2.5 cm, reduced <u>IVC</u> collapsibility   [[30]](/library/aibQJt)

* <u>Heart</u> 

* Reduced systolic function in patients with <u>HFrEF</u>

* Other: <u>pericardial effusion</u>, features suggestive of an underlying etiology (e.g., <u>cardiac tamponade</u>, <u>right ventricular</u> dilation in <u>PE</u>) [[31]](/library/bibHJt)

> [!TIP]
> Perform a rapid assessment with bedside <u>echocardiography</u> and other <u>POCUS</u> techniques to quickly establish the underlying cause of acute <u>dyspnea</u> and/or <u>shock</u>.




### Advanced imaging




If more detailed information about <u>myocardial</u> viability and/or <u>perfusion</u> is needed (e.g., procedural planning, <u>myocardial</u> <u>ischemia</u> is suspected), further imaging modalities may be necessary after the patient is stabilized. Both <u>MRI</u> and CT require the patient to lie flat for sustained periods and are less accurate at higher <u>heart rates</u>.




* <u>Cardiac MRI</u> (<u>CMR</u>) [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

* May show evidence of <u>fibrosis</u>, <u>cardiomyopathy</u>, or <u>perfusion</u> defects

* Can be used to assess <u>LVEF</u>

* <u>Cardiac CT</u>: assessment of <u>coronary arteries</u> (e.g., in suspected <u>ischemic heart disease</u>) and structural defects [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

* <u>Stress</u> imaging  [[25]](/library/LSbwZt)

* For suspected <u>ischemic</u> etiology or valvular pathology

* Findings may include: wall motion abnormalities, reduced coronary flow, <u>myocardial</u> deformation, <u>interstitial</u> fluid

* <u>Coronary angiography</u>: to evaluate for <u>ischemic cardiomyopathy</u> [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

## Management

### Initial management [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)[[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)




* Perform a rapid <u>ABCDE survey</u> to assess hemodynamic stability.

* Identify and treat any acute underlying cause of AHF for all patients (e.g., consider <u>PCI</u> for patients with <u>ACS</u>).





#### Hemodynamically stable patients




* Clinical presentation

* <u>SBP</u> > 90 mm Hg and no <u>signs of end-organ hypoperfusion</u>

* Respiratory <u>distress</u> may be present.

* Management

* All patients: Start or continue <u>SGLT2i</u> therapy. [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)

* Patients with no evidence of congestion (dry and warm): Optimize oral pharmacotherapy.

* Patients with evidence of congestion (wet and warm)

* Provide <u>respiratory support in AHF</u>;  (e.g., positioning, <u>supplemental O<sub>2</sub></u>) as needed.

* Start <u>diuretic therapy for AHF</u> if there is <u>volume overload</u>.

* Consider <u>vasodilators for AHF</u>, e.g., <u>nitrates</u>.

* <u>Morphine</u> is not recommended. [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)[[34]](/library/SpYyKJ)

* Next steps

* Clinical improvement

* Optimize <u>guideline-directed medical therapy</u> and begin <u>supportive care</u> (see “Ongoing hospital management”).

* Consider hospital admission vs. discharge home in patients presenting to the emergency department (see “Disposition”).

* Clinical deterioration: See “<u>Hemodynamically unstable</u> patients.”





> [!NOTE]
> To remember the management of <u>ADHF</u>, think of “LMNOP”: Loop <u>diuretics</u> (<u>furosemide</u>), Modify medications, Nitrates, Oxygen if <u>hypoxic</u>, Position (with elevated upper body). [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)[[34]](/library/SpYyKJ)




> [!TIP]
> For patients with <u>ACS</u> complicated by acute <u>heart failure</u>, consult cardiology for consideration of urgent <u>coronary catheterization</u>.




#### <u>Hemodynamically unstable</u> patients [[35]](/library/ipYJ6J)




Early specialist consultation (e.g., critical care, cardiology) and admission to hospital is recommended.




* Clinical presentation: can vary

* <u>Cardiogenic shock</u>: <u>SBP</u> < 90 mm Hg OR <u>signs of end-organ hypoperfusion</u>

* <u>Hypertensive emergency</u>: <u>hypertension</u> (e.g., <u>SBP</u> > 180 mm Hg) PLUS <u>flash pulmonary edema</u> and <u>hypoxemic respiratory failure</u>

* Management: depends on the <u>classification of AHF</u> (See also “<u>Hemodynamic support for AHF</u>” and “<u>Management of cardiogenic shock</u>.”)

* Evidence of congestion with <u>shock</u> (wet and cold)

* Prioritize <u>respiratory support for AHF</u>.

* Consider <u>inotropic</u> support (e.g., <u>dobutamine</u>, <u>norepinephrine</u>).

* <u>Shock</u> without evidence of congestion (dry and cold): Consider <u>fluid challenge</u>; add <u>vasopressors and inotropes</u> for <u>shock</u> refractory to fluids.

* <u>Hypertensive emergency</u> with <u>flash pulmonary edema</u> (wet and warm)

* Begin <u>NIPPV</u> and <u>vasodilators for AHF</u>.  [[34]](/library/SpYyKJ)[[36]](/library/kibm7t)[[37]](/library/xycEhU0)

* Identify and treat the underlying trigger: e.g., poorly controlled <u>hypertension</u>, <u>arrhythmias</u>, <u>acute coronary syndrome</u>, <u>valvular heart disease</u>. [[38]](/library/35YSPp)[[39]](/library/oAc0kU0)

* Next steps

* Clinical improvement: Once stabilized, start <u>diuretics for AHF</u>, initiate or adjust <u>pharmacotherapy for HF</u>, and begin <u>supportive care</u> (see “Ongoing hospital management”).

* Clinical deterioration: See “Treatment of refractory <u>heart failure</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with a wet and cold clinical presentation have a high risk of rapid deterioration and require close <u>hemodynamic monitoring</u> regardless of their blood pressure. [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)




> [!TIP]
> If <u>atrial fibrillation</u> is thought to be causing hemodynamic or respiratory instability, consider immediate <u>electric cardioversion</u>.




### Ongoing hospital management [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)




#### <u>Supportive care</u>




* Fluid restriction does not reduce hospitalization or <u>mortality rates</u> in patients with HF. [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

* <u>Sodium</u> restriction  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

* Discontinue or avoid any <u>drugs that may worsen HF</u> (e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>, <u>thiazolidinediones</u>) [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)[[34]](/library/SpYyKJ)

* Identify and treat comorbidities (e.g., <u>atrial fibrillation</u>, <u>pneumonia</u>, <u>COPD</u>) and underlying triggers.

* <u>VTE prophylaxis</u>  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[40]](/library/z8Yr6I)

* For large volume <u>ascites</u>, consider <u>therapeutic paracentesis</u>.  [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)[[41]](/library/WJWPGm0)





#### Optimizing therapy for chronic HF [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)[[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)




* Administer <u>beta blockers</u> cautiously in <u>beta-blocker</u>-naive patients.

* Start at a low dose (see “<u>Medical treatment of heart failure</u>” for dosages).

* Administer only after stabilization (i.e., once the patient is hemodynamically stable without significant congestion, <u>diuretic</u> dose is stable, and <u>vasodilators</u> and <u>inotropic</u> agents have been discontinued).  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)[[34]](/library/SpYyKJ)

* Optimize <u>guideline-directed medical therapy</u>.

* Initiate or continue <u>SGLT2i</u> therapy.

* Patients on a stable dose of <u>beta blockers</u>: Continue the same dosage.  [[3]](/library/5xYiCr)

* Consider switching from <u>ACEIs</u> or <u>ARBs</u> to an <u>ARNI</u> if blood pressure is stable. [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)

* Significant decline in renal function: Consider reducing or stopping <u>RAAS inhibitors</u>, <u>aldosterone antagonists</u>, and <u>digoxin</u>.

* <u>Hypotension</u>: Consider discontinuing <u>hydralazine</u>/<u>isosorbide dinitrate</u>, <u>RAAS inhibitors</u>, and <u>beta blockers</u>.

* <u>Bradycardia</u>: Consider reducing or discontinuing <u>beta blockers</u> and <u>digoxin</u>.

* Optimize blood pressure control (see “<u>Hypertension</u>”).





> [!TIP]
> For patients not previously on <u>beta blockers</u>, use cautiously and only once the patient has been stabilized.




#### Monitoring [[3]](/library/5xYiCr)[[7]](/library/-p1DH30)




* Daily weights, intake, and output monitoring

* Check renal function and <u>electrolytes</u> every 12–24 hours (see “<u>Diuretic therapy in acute heart failure</u>”)

* Consider serial <u>BNP</u> or <u>NT-proBNP</u> measurement.  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)[[42]](/library/_lb5zF)

* Consider <u>invasive hemodynamic monitoring</u>.

* <u>POCUS</u> can be used to monitor <u>volume overload</u>. [[43]](/library/AlbRzF)





### Treatment of refractory acute heart failure [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)




Consider the following if AHF persists despite maximal respiratory and <u>hemodynamic support</u>.




* Alternative diagnoses and comorbidities: See “<u>Differential diagnosis of dyspnea</u>” and “<u>Differential diagnosis of peripheral edema</u>.” [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)

* <u>Ultrafiltration</u>:  (e.g., <u>hemodialysis</u>): indicated in congestion with no response to medical therapy [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)

* <u>Mechanical circulatory support</u>: indicated in reversible refractory acute <u>heart failure</u> [[35]](/library/ipYJ6J)[[44]](/library/fxYkDr)

* <u>ECMO</u> is the most widely used form of mechanical support in acute <u>heart failure</u>.

* <u>Intra-aortic balloon pump</u> and <u>left ventricular assist device</u> may be useful in certain etiologies, e.g., <u>mitral regurgitation</u>.

* Management of effusions: Consider <u>therapeutic thoracentesis</u> or <u>pericardiocentesis</u> as needed.

---

## Respiratory support

The cornerstones of <u>respiratory support in acute heart failure</u> are <u>oxygen therapy</u> and <u>positive pressure ventilation</u>, typically starting with the least invasive modality and escalating as needed. [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)




### Initial measures [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)




* Positioning: Ensure the patient is sitting upright.    [[47]](/library/YxYnEr)

* <u>Supplemental oxygen</u>: indicated for patients with an <u>SpO<sub>2</sub></u> < 90% or <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u> < 60 mm Hg (see “<u>Oxygen therapy</u>”).





### <u>Respiratory failure</u>




* <u>High-flow nasal cannula</u> (<u>HFNC</u>): Consider in patients with an <u>SpO<sub>2</sub></u> < 90% non-responsive to <u>basic oxygen delivery systems</u>. [[48]](/library/Dib1Ft)[[49]](/library/wkbhJF)[[50]](/library/9kbNJF)[[51]](/library/CkbqJF)

* <u>NIPPV</u>: for patients with <u>respiratory distress</u> despite <u>supplemental oxygen</u>  [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)

* <u>CPAP</u> is preferred over <u>BiPAP</u>. [[52]](/library/Eld8AJ0)

* Avoid in patients with isolated <u>RV failure</u> , severe <u>hypotension</u>  [[53]](/library/yibd8t)

* <u>Invasive mechanical ventilation</u>

* Indications

* <u>Hypoxemic respiratory failure</u> unresponsive to <u>NIPPV</u>

* Refractory <u>hypoxemia</u> (<u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u> < 60 mm Hg)

* <u>Hypercapnia</u> (<u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u> > 50 mm Hg)

* <u>Acidosis</u> (<u>pH</u> < 7.35)

* <u>Intubation</u> and <u>mechanical ventilation</u> in patients with acute <u>heart failure</u> can be challenging.  [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)[[41]](/library/WJWPGm0)

* See “<u>High-risk indications for mechanical ventilation</u>” and “<u>Hemodynamic compromise in mechanically ventilated patients</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> <u>EPAP</u> and/or <u>PEEP</u> should be used with caution in patients with hemodynamic compromise.

---

## Pharmacotherapy

See also “<u>Pharmacotherapy for chronic HF</u>.”




### Diuretic therapy in acute heart failure [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)




All hemodynamically stable patients with evidence of congestion (wet and warm) require <u>diuretic</u> therapy.




#### Initial treatment




* Administer <u>diuretics</u> intravenously, if possible.

* <u>Diuretic</u>-naive patients: IV <u>furosemide</u> DOSAGE OR <u>bumetanide</u> DOSAGE [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)

* Patients already taking <u>diuretics</u>: Administer 1–2.5 times the patient's usual oral dose intravenously as a bolus or continuous infusion. [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)





#### Continuing treatment




* <u>Loop diuretic</u> adjustment

* Assess the effect of <u>diuretics</u> (e.g., urine output, urine <u>sodium</u> level, symptoms of congestion) every 6 hours.  [[54]](/library/7ib4Gt)[[55]](/library/t_0XJi)

* Urinary output < 100 mL/hour or urine <u>sodium</u> < 50 mEq/L: Consider doubling the <u>diuretic</u> dose.  [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)

* Urinary output > 100–150 mL/hour or urine <u>sodium</u> â¥ 50 mEq/L

* Patients with continued congestion (e.g., <u>pulmonary edema</u>): Continue scheduled <u>diuretic</u> at the current dose.

* Patients with no residual congestion: Consider less frequent dosing or transition to an oral <u>diuretic</u>.

* Refractory congestion: Consult a cardiologist and consider adding any of the following. 

* A <u>thiazide diuretic</u>, e.g., <u>metolazone</u> DOSAGE, <u>hydrochlorothiazide</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE, <u>chlorothiazide</u> DOSAGE [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)[[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[54]](/library/7ib4Gt)

* <u>Acetazolamide</u> DOSAGE [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)[[56]](/library/vldAAJ0)

* <u>Vasodilators for AHF</u> [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

* Low-dose <u>dopamine infusion</u>  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[57]](/library/Fvcgbe0)

* Transition to oral <u>diuretic</u> [[5]](/library/-RbDpt)

* Once the patient is <u>euvolemic</u> and at their functional baseline

* <u>Furosemide</u> oral dose is double the <u>furosemide</u> IV dose.

* <u>Bumetanide</u> oral and IV dosing are equivalent.





> [!WARNING]
> Use <u>diuretics</u> judiciously and assess <u>volume status</u>, <u>electrolytes</u>, and <u>creatinine</u> levels regularly to avoid overaggressive diuresis, as this may lead to <u>hypotension</u>, <u>electrolyte</u> imbalances, and/or a deterioration in <u>kidney function</u>. [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)[[7]](/library/-p1DH30)




#### Monitoring




* Monitor and <u>replete serum electrolytes</u> (e.g., <u>potassium</u>, <u>magnesium</u>, <u>sodium</u>) every 12–24 hours.

* Monitor <u>kidney function</u> (<u>creatinine</u> levels) at least once daily until the patient is stable.

* Consider <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Elevated <u>creatinine</u> is not a contraindication to <u>diuretic</u> therapy in patients with acute <u>heart failure</u>, as renal function typically improves with effective diuresis in <u>cardiorenal syndrome</u>. [[58]](/library/2pYTKJ)




### <u>SGLT2is</u> [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)




* Indications: hemodynamically stable patients with estimated <u>GFR</u> ≥ 20 mL/min/m<sup>2</sup>, regardless of <u>LVEF</u>

* Agents: <u>dapagliflozin</u> DOSAGE, <u>empagliflozin</u> DOSAGE

* Considerations: Reassess <u>diuretic</u> dosing when starting <u>SGLT2is</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Early initiation of <u>SGLT2i</u> therapy in patients hospitalized with acute <u>heart failure</u> decreases <u>major cardiovascular events</u> and congestion, and reduces the length of hospital stay. [[4]](/library/8ldOAJ0)[[59]](/library/vNdA1q0)[[60]](/library/mUdVd60)




### Vasodilator therapy in acute heart failure




* Indications  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)[[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)

* Acute <u>heart failure</u> caused by <u>hypertensive emergency</u> (see “<u>Treatment of hypertensive crises</u>”) [[9]](/library/bmWHVN0)[[61]](/library/OzaIGM)

* <u>Flash pulmonary edema</u>

* Adjuvant to <u>diuretics</u> for symptomatic relief of <u>dyspnea</u> [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

* Treatment options  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

* IV <u>nitroglycerin</u> DOSAGE  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

* <u>Sodium nitroprusside</u> DOSAGE  [[7]](/library/-p1DH30)

* Cautions

* Do not use <u>vasodilators</u> if <u>SBP</u> is < 90 mm Hg.

* Doses should be carefully titrated to prevent large drops in blood pressure. [[62]](/library/VlbGDF)

* Use with caution in patients with mitral or <u>aortic stenosis</u>. [[63]](/library/POaWsk)





> [!TIP]
> For patients with hypertensive acute <u>heart failure</u> with <u>pulmonary edema</u> in the emergency department or prehospital setting, consider a single dose of sublingual <u>nitroglycerin</u> (i.e., <u>nitroglycerin</u> 0.4 mg sublingual once) while obtaining <u>IV access</u> and setting up an infusion. [[34]](/library/SpYyKJ)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid the use of <u>vasodilators</u> in patients with acute <u>heart failure</u> and <u>hypotension</u>.
